386.title: Tzav: first, the ashes (Leviticus 6:3–4)
386.hook: each day the priest begins by clearing yesterday's ashes, in plain clothes
386.howItsDone: The lifting of the ashes, terumat ha-deshen, is described in the Mishnah's tractates Tamid and Yoma, and some prayer books include its passages among the morning readings about the Temple service.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the altar fire that must never go out. Your line was keep the fire. Today, the first job of the priest's day.

In the sanctuary, as the rabbis describe the day, the first job wasn't a grand prayer or a beautiful offering. It was cleaning. Before anything new could happen on the altar, someone had to deal with what was left from yesterday. The fire had burned all night, and there were ashes. And the Torah gives that humble job careful instructions, right down to what the priest should wear.
screen: `THE FIRST JOB OF THE DAY.` → `NOT A PRAYER. CLEANING.` → `RIGHT DOWN TO THE CLOTHES.`

segments.voice: Here's what the verses describe. The priest puts on his linen priestly garments, lifts a portion of the ashes from the altar and sets it beside the altar. Then he takes off those garments, puts on others, and carries the rest of the ashes out of the camp, to a clean place. The rabbis called this terumat ha-deshen, the lifting of the ashes, and it was the first act of the Temple day. Notice the two changes of clothes. Lifting the ashes at the altar is done in full priestly linen: this dirty job counts as holy service. For hauling them out, the priest changes into plainer clothes. Rashi explains with a picture from a household: the clothes a servant wears to cook a pot for his master aren't the clothes he wears to pour his master's wine. Each job gets the right clothes, and both are service. Then the Mishnah adds a story. In the Temple, this job was so sought after that priests would race up the ramp of the altar to win it; whoever got within four cubits first won. Once, two were neck and neck, one pushed the other, and he fell and broke his leg. After that, the court decided it by lottery. Grown men, competing to be the one who cleans up. The day's holiness began with yesterday's ashes, cleared first, and cleared gladly.

segments.voice: Picture the space where you'll be today, your desk, your kitchen, your car, your inbox, and find one small patch of what's left from yesterday. Picture clearing it carefully, as the first act of the day, not a chore to resent but the job that makes room for what's new. If there's inner ash too, an old irritation, notice it, and set it down.
Tzav. Command. The portion where every day in the sanctuary begins by clearing yesterday's ashes.
Your line: clear the ashes first. Even the cleanup can be holy work. Three hundred eighty-six days in.

387.title: Tzav: the thanks offering (Leviticus 7:12)
387.hook: after a rescue, a thanks offering; midrash says thanks alone will never cease
387.howItsDone: A person who has come through danger, such as serious illness, a dangerous journey or release from captivity, recites the blessing ha-gomel at the Torah reading, and the congregation responds.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the priest's first job: lifting yesterday's ashes. Your line was clear the ashes first. Today, an everyday word with an old story inside.

Spend an hour in an Israeli supermarket, a taxi or a café, and today's word comes at you again and again. Todah. It's how you say thank you in Hebrew: todah for the change, todah for the coffee, todah rabbah, thanks a lot. But before it was the word at the checkout counter, it was the name of an offering. A very particular one, brought by a very particular kind of person: someone who had just been rescued.
screen: `TODAH: THANK YOU.` → `AT THE CHECKOUT, IN THE TAXI.` → `FIRST, AN OFFERING.`

segments.voice: Leviticus lists a family of offerings called peace offerings, and the first kind is this one: "If he offer it for a thanksgiving." Who brings it? Rashi, drawing on the Talmud's reading of Psalm one hundred seven, names four kinds of people who come through danger: those who cross the sea, those who cross the desert, those who recover from serious illness, and those set free from prison. Each has been rescued, and the todah is how they say so. The offering came with a lot of bread, forty loaves by the rabbis' count, and the Torah says it all had to be eaten the same day and night. Some commentators point out the result: you couldn't eat forty loaves alone. You had to invite people in, and over the meal you'd tell them what happened. The thanks became a party, and the party became a story. Then a midrash in Leviticus Rabbah says that in the time to come, all the offerings will cease except the thanks offering, and all the prayers will cease except the prayer of thanks. The idea seems to be that when everything is mended, no one will need to ask for anything or atone for anything, but people will still say thank you. Today, with no Temple, the custom lives on in a blessing called ha-gomel, said in synagogue by someone who has come through danger, with the congregation answering.

segments.voice: Think of a time you came through something: a scary diagnosis that turned out fine, a near miss on the road, a hard year, a moment someone pulled you out. Remember it clearly, without rushing: who helped, and what could have happened, and didn't? If you pray, say todah to God; if not, say it to the people who were there, even just in your mind.
Todah. Thanks. The offering brought after a rescue, and still the everyday Hebrew word for thank you.
Your line: thanks outlasts everything. A rescue is worth a table full of guests. Day three hundred eighty-seven.

388.title: Tzav: ear, thumb, toe (Leviticus 8:23–24)
388.hook: priests are anointed on the ear, the thumb and the big toe: hear, do, walk
388.tomorrow: Tzav: seven days at the door
388.howItsDone: The ordination ceremony of Leviticus 8 is read in the portion Tzav, and the same ear, thumb and toe rite appears in Leviticus 14 for a person healed of tzara'at.

segments.voice: Yesterday, todah, the thanks offering brought after a rescue. Your line was thanks outlasts everything. Today, the priests are ordained, with three surprising marks.

Designing a ceremony to make someone a priest, where would you put the mark? The forehead, maybe, like a crown. The heart. The hands that will do the work. The Torah picks three places few would guess: the edge of the right ear, the thumb of the right hand, and the big toe of the right foot. It sounds almost comic, until you stop and ask what those three have in common, and what they leave out.
screen: `WHERE WOULD YOU PUT THE MARK?` → `NOT THE HEAD, NOT THE HEART.` → `EAR, THUMB, BIG TOE.`

segments.voice: It's the week of the priests' ordination. Moses, acting as priest himself for these days, brings a ram called the ram of consecration and takes some of its blood. He puts it "upon the tip of Aaron's right ear, and upon the thumb of his right hand, and upon the great toe of his right foot," then does the same for each of Aaron's sons. The Torah doesn't explain the choice. Commentators have read it as a map of a life of service. The ear, to listen: to God, and to the people who come with their troubles. The hand, to do the work. The foot, to walk the right path and go where you're needed. Listening first, then doing, then walking, and the order runs from top to bottom: the whole body, claimed for service. Then a surprise from later in Leviticus. The same marking, ear, thumb and toe, is done for someone else: a person healed from the skin affliction called tzara'at, who had been living outside the camp and is now coming home. The priest starting his service and the outcast returning to the community receive the same three touches. Some readers take the pairing as a sign the marking isn't about rank, but about a person beginning again, with ears, hands and feet given a new purpose.
screen: `THE RAM OF CONSECRATION.` · `EAR, THUMB AND BIG TOE.` · `LISTEN, THEN DO, THEN WALK.` · `THE SAME MARK FOR ONE RETURNING.` · then, large: `LISTEN, DO, WALK.`

segments.voice: Touch your right ear gently and ask what you need to listen for today, and who needs you to listen. Touch your right thumb and ask what your hands should do; then press your right big toe to the floor and ask where you need to go, or not go. Take a breath with each, then sit with all three, ready.
Tzav. Command. The portion where the priests are ordained, marked on the right ear, the right thumb and the right big toe.
Your line: listen, do, walk. Ear, hand and foot, all given to the work. Until tomorrow.

389.title: Tzav: seven days at the door (Leviticus 8:33–35)
389.hook: the priests wait seven days at the entrance before serving
389.howItsDone: Following the Talmud's reading of these verses, the high priest in the Second Temple was set apart for seven days before Yom Kippur to prepare for the day's service.

segments.voice: Yesterday, in Tzav, the new priests were marked on ear, thumb and toe. Your line was listen, do, walk. Today, they're ready, and told to wait.

The robes are on. The oil has been poured on Aaron's head. The blood is on ear, thumb and toe. Everything is ready. In a movie, the next scene would be Aaron striding into the sanctuary to begin his life's work. Instead, Moses gives the new priests an instruction that sounds almost like a letdown. Don't go anywhere. Stay right here, at the entrance of the tent, day and night. Not for an hour. For a week. The work they've been dressed for will have to wait.
screen: `ROBES ON, OIL POURED.` → `READY TO BEGIN.` → `INSTEAD: STAY AT THE ENTRANCE.`

segments.voice: The verses say: you shall not go out from the entrance of the tent of meeting for seven days, until the days of your ordination are complete. Stay at the entrance day and night, and keep the charge of the Lord. The Hebrew for these days of ordination is milu'im, from a root meaning filling. In biblical Hebrew, to ordain a priest is literally to fill his hands. So these are filling days: not days of doing, but days of being filled. What were they doing at the door all week? The text doesn't say much. The offerings were repeated each day, and the priests ate their portion at the entrance. Mostly, they waited, in the doorway between the camp and the holy place, neither outside nor fully in. And seven isn't a random number. It's the length of creation, the week every Jew lives by. The rabbis took this week seriously enough to build on it. The Talmud, at the start of the tractate on Yom Kippur, learns from these verses that the high priest should be set apart for seven days before the holiest day of the year, to prepare. The Mishnah sets apart the priest who burned the red heifer for seven days as well. Here, the holiest work doesn't start the moment someone is ready. It starts after a week in the doorway, hands being filled.
screen: `DON'T LEAVE THE ENTRANCE.` · `MILU'IM: FILLING THE HANDS.` · `A WEEK IN THE DOORWAY.` · `SEVEN DAYS BEFORE YOM KIPPUR.` · then, large: `WAIT AT THE DOOR.`

segments.voice: Think of something big you're about to start, or want to: a move, a project, a hard conversation, a new habit. Instead of planning it, stand at its entrance for a minute, and notice what you hope for and what you're afraid of. Rest your hands open in your lap, empty, the way the priests' hands were before they were filled.
Tzav. Command. The portion that ends with the new priests waiting seven days at the entrance of the tent, before they serve.
Your line: wait at the door. A pause at the threshold is part of the work. That's day three hundred eighty-nine.

390.title: Shemini: the eighth day (Leviticus 9:1)
390.hook: after seven days of preparation, the service begins on the eighth
390.howItsDone: The priestly blessing that tradition links to Aaron's first blessing on the eighth day is still recited in synagogues by kohanim, descendants of Aaron, with hands raised toward the congregation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the new priests stood seven days in the doorway. Your line was wait at the door. Today, a new portion, and the waiting ends.

Seven is the number of a complete week: six days of work, one of rest, and then it starts over. Shabbat keeps that loop turning. So what's an eighth day? In Jewish life, it keeps showing up when something new begins. A baby boy is brought into the covenant on his eighth day. The festival of Sukkot is followed by an eighth day of its own. And this week's portion is named for it: Shemini, eighth. After a week of waiting at the door, the priests finally step through.
screen: `SEVEN: A COMPLETE WEEK.` → `THE EIGHTH DAY KEEPS SHOWING UP.` → `SHEMINI: EIGHTH.`

segments.voice: It opens: "And it came to pass on the eighth day, that Moses called Aaron and his sons, and the elders of Israel." The rabbis say this was the first day of Nisan, the day the sanctuary was set up for good. The Talmud says that day took ten crowns, the first of many things: the first day the priests served, the first day the people's offerings were brought there, the first day God's presence rested among them. Moses tells Aaron what to bring, and why: for today the LORD appears to you. Then Aaron, who has watched for seven days, does it himself for the first time: the offering for himself, the offering for the people. When it's done, Aaron lifts his hands toward the people and blesses them. Rashi says this was the priestly blessing, still said in synagogues today: may the Lord bless you and keep you. Moses and Aaron go into the tent together, come out, and bless the people again. The glory of the Lord appears to everyone. Fire comes out and consumes the offering on the altar, and the people see it, shout for joy and fall on their faces. Why does so much begin on an eighth day? Some teachers say seven is the natural world, complete in itself, and eight is one step beyond it: the place where the holy breaks in.

391.title: Shemini: strange fire (Leviticus 10:1–2)
391.hook: Nadav and Avihu bring fire not commanded and die; commentators still ask why
391.howItsDone: The death of Nadav and Avihu is read in the portion Shemini and again in the Torah reading for Yom Kippur morning, which opens 'after the death of the two sons of Aaron'.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the eighth day: the priests began to serve, and fire came down on the altar. Your line was the eighth day begins. Today, a hard turn.

Yesterday ended in joy: the sanctuary working at last, Aaron blessing the people, fire from God consuming the offering, the whole camp shouting for joy. Then, with almost no pause, the very next verse turns everything over. Today's story is a hard one. It's only two verses long, and it doesn't explain itself. Readers have argued about it ever since. There's no solving it today, only looking at it honestly.
screen: `JOY ON THE EIGHTH DAY.` → `THEN, THE NEXT VERSE.` → `TWO VERSES, NO EXPLANATION.`

segments.voice: Here it is: "And Nadab and Abihu, the sons of Aaron, took each of them his censer, and put fire therein, and laid incense thereon, and offered strange fire before the LORD, which He had not commanded them. And there came forth fire from before the LORD, and devoured them, and they died before the LORD." Aaron's two oldest sons, on the day of their father's first service. The text uses the very words it used one verse earlier for the fire that consumed the offering: fire from before the LORD. What did they do wrong? The only clue is fire which He had not commanded them. The rabbis offered many answers, and Rashi records two. One sage says they made a ruling of their own in front of Moses, their teacher, instead of asking him. Another says they came in drunk, since a few verses later priests are forbidden wine before serving. A midrash in Leviticus Rabbah lists still more. And some later commentators read it almost the opposite way: the brothers weren't wicked at all, but so full of love for God that they rushed too close, like moths to a flame, and couldn't come back. What these readings share, from the harshest to the most tender: the brothers acted on their own fire. Not God's command, not their teacher's word, not the careful plan these chapters have followed. Passion, or pride, or love; it wasn't listening. And that's as far as honesty can go. The Torah doesn't say more, and it would be dishonest to pretend it does.
screen: `STRANGE FIRE, NOT COMMANDED.` · `A RULING BEFORE THEIR TEACHER?` · `TOO CLOSE, OUT OF LOVE?` · `THEIR OWN FIRE, NOT LISTENING.` · then, large: `ZEAL WITHOUT LISTENING.`

segments.voice: Let Nadav and Avihu's story rest in front of you without choosing an explanation, and if an urge comes to settle it, to decide it was deserved or unfair, let that be there too. Then, gently, think of a time your own enthusiasm ran ahead of your listening, and what it cost, without judging it. Breathe slowly, and hold the question open.
Shemini. Eighth. The portion where the eighth day's joy is broken by strange fire, and the Torah leaves us asking why.
Your line: zeal without listening. Some questions are meant to stay open. See you tomorrow.

options: Only that their fire wasn't commanded. The rabbis offer many reasons; the text leaves it open.
Yes: it says they forgot the incense, so the fire on their pans had nothing to burn.
No, and they lived on afterward; the fire from God was only a warning to them.
chat.meaning: The text's only clue is fire which He had not commanded. Rashi records two views, the midrash more, and the Torah itself says no more.

392.title: Shemini: Aaron's silence (Leviticus 10:3)
392.hook: after his sons die, "Aaron held his peace"
392.howItsDone: When Jews visit a house of mourning during shiva, the seven days after a burial, custom holds that visitors sit quietly and wait for the mourner to speak first, and the conversation follows the mourner's lead.

segments.voice: Yesterday, strange fire: Nadav and Avihu, and a story with no easy answer. Your line was zeal without listening. Today, their father.

A visit to a house of mourning often has a moment at the door: a sentence rehearsed in the car, then the person's face, and every prepared word sounds wrong. It's tempting to talk anyway, because silence can feel like failure. Leviticus has a scene like that, only the one who can't find words is the father. On the great day of dedication, fire consumed Aaron's two eldest sons. Moses turns to his brother with a hard theological sentence. And the Torah gives Aaron's answer in two Hebrew words, which say only that he was still.
screen: `THE MOMENT AT THE DOOR.` → `THE GREAT DAY, AND TWO SONS GONE.` → `AARON'S ANSWER.`

segments.voice: Start with what Moses said. The Lord had spoken, he tells Aaron, of being sanctified through those who are near. Rashi hears Moses trying to comfort: I knew this house would be made holy through someone close to God; I thought it would be you or me; now I see your sons were greater than us both. Then, what Aaron did: "And Aaron held his peace." In Hebrew, vayidom Aharon. The verb means to be still; a psalm uses the same word for being still before God and waiting. It isn't described as calm. It's described as quiet. Rashi notes that Aaron was rewarded for that silence: a few verses later, God speaks to Aaron directly, without Moses in between. Commentators have read the silence many ways: acceptance, shock, a grief too big for speech, even a protest held back. The text doesn't say which. And it shaped how mourners are visited. Jewish law teaches that visitors to a house of shiva wait for the mourner to speak first. In the book of Job, before the long speeches begin, his friends sit with him seven days and seven nights, and none of them says a word. A closed mouth and a chair pulled close can be the whole visit.
screen: `MOSES TRIES TO EXPLAIN.` · `VAYIDOM AHARON: AARON WAS STILL.` · `A SILENCE THE TEXT DOESN'T EXPLAIN.` · `AT SHIVA, THE MOURNER SPEAKS FIRST.` · then, large: `AND AARON HELD HIS PEACE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone in your life who is carrying a loss, and keep them company in your mind, without planning what to say and without fixing anything. If no one comes to mind, sit with Aaron at the edge of the camp, and let the quiet be enough.
Shemini, the eighth: the portion where the great day turns to grief, and Aaron holds his peace.
Your line: and Aaron held his peace. Sometimes being there is the whole answer. Another week of Leviticus behind you now.

original.note: Hebrew: "and Aaron was still." from the root d-m-m, to be silent, to be still.

trapdoor: what you thought: Aaron kept calm.
what it means: the text records only silence, and leaves what was inside it unexplained.
what a scholar hears: d-m-m is a stillness word, not a calm word; Rashi ties the silence to Leviticus 10:8, where God speaks to Aaron alone.
guess: eighth: the portion of the first service day

chat.says: A friend just lost her dad. What do I even say when I visit?
options: Maybe nothing at first. At shiva, visitors let the mourner speak first, as Aaron was still.
Explain why it happened. Moses did that for Aaron, and it's what helps most.
Keep talking so there's no silence, since quiet makes a mourner feel alone.
chat.meaning: Aaron met his loss with silence, and Jewish law teaches shiva visitors to wait for the mourner to speak first. Job's friends sat seven days without a word.
